title: Vectors as positions, displacements and features
goal: Separate a geometric position from a feature vector, and calculate vector operations with units in mind.
exercises: Find the displacement from (1,4) to (4,2).
For u=(2,-1), v=(1,3), calculate 3u-2v.
Flatten [[1,2],[3,4]] in row order and state its vector dimension.
Why might raw distance between [brightness, width] be misleading?
solutions: Subtract start from end: (4-1,2-4)=(3,-2).
The vector is [1,2,3,4], with four coordinates. A column representation has shape (4,1).
Different units and numerical scales can make one coordinate dominate. Fit scaling using training data, or choose a justified metric.
checkpoint: Explain what every coordinate of a toy image feature means. Give a position, a displacement, and a feature vector without confusing their roles.

title: Norms, dot products, angles and projections
goal: Derive length, similarity and orthogonal projection from coordinate calculations.
exercises: Find the L1 and L2 norms of (-3,4).
Compute the cosine similarity of (1,0) and (1,1).
Project (2,3) onto u=(1,0), and give the residual.
Can the zero vector be normalized to a unit vector? Explain.
solutions: The dot product is 1 and the norm product is sqrt(2), so cosine=1/sqrt(2).
c=2, projection=(2,0), residual=(0,3). Its dot product with u is zero.
No. Dividing by its norm divides by zero; it has no defined direction.
checkpoint: Derive the projection coefficient from residual orthogonality, then explain when cosine similarity loses information a classifier might need.

title: Matrices as maps and composition
goal: Interpret matrix columns geometrically and track dimensions through a linear layer.
exercises: Apply [[2,0],[0,3]] to the column vector (1,-2).
If X=(16,64) and W=(64,10), give the output and bias shapes.
For A=(3,2) and B=(4,3), which product is defined and what is its shape?
Is f(x)=2x+1 a linear map? Justify with f(0).
solutions: The result is (2,-6).
XW has shape (16,10); a bias of shape (10,) broadcasts across samples.
BA is defined, with shape (4,2). AB is undefined because 2 and 4 do not match.
It is affine. f(0)=1, whereas a linear map must send zero to zero.
checkpoint: Explain a matrix product using its columns, then annotate every shape in a batch affine layer without executing code.

title: Independence, bases, rank and null spaces
goal: Connect independent directions and rank to information preserved or discarded.
exercises: Are (1,2) and (3,6) independent? Give a relation.
Find the rank and a null vector of [[1,1],[2,2]].
A linear map has 5 inputs and rank 3. What is its null-space dimension?
Why can a 2x4 map never have an inverse recovering every four-coordinate input?
solutions: They are dependent: 3*(1,2)-(3,6)=0.
Rank=1; (1,-1) is a nonzero null vector.
Rank-nullity gives 5-3=2.
Its rank is at most 2, so its null-space dimension is at least 2. Different inputs share outputs.
checkpoint: Construct two different inputs with the same output under a rank-deficient map. Explain precisely what prevents recovery.

title: Exact, inconsistent and underdetermined systems
goal: Decide whether a measurement system has zero, one or many solutions.
exercises: Solve x+y=5 and x-y=1.
Are x+2y=3 and 2x+4y=8 consistent?
Describe all solutions of x-y=2.
Write the design matrix for fitting y=a*t+c at t=0,1,2.
solutions: Adding gives x=3; substituting gives y=2.
No. Doubling the first equation requires right-hand side 6, but the second requires 8.
Let y=t freely; then x=t+2, so (x,y)=(t+2,t).
A=[[0,1],[1,1],[2,1]] and the unknown column is (a,c). The observed y values form b.
checkpoint: Classify one system of each kind and justify it using column space and null space, rather than only counting equations.

title: Least squares as projection
goal: Derive residual orthogonality and fit a line to inconsistent observations.
exercises: Fit a constant c to observations [1,2,6] by least squares.
For the worked line fit, calculate the residual sum and sum of squared residuals.
Why is b-A*theta orthogonal to the column space at an optimum?
Does a residual sum of zero imply every observation is fit exactly?
solutions: The projection onto the constant column gives c=(1+2+6)/3=3.
Otherwise a move within that space could remove a component of the error and reduce its squared length.
No. Residuals [-1,1] sum to zero while squared error is 2.
checkpoint: Set up an unseen line fit, identify the column space, and verify the residual is orthogonal to its columns.

title: QR, pseudoinverses and numerical conditioning
goal: Understand why mathematically valid formulas can be numerically unreliable.
exercises: Solve R*theta=(5,3) for R=[[2,1],[0,3]].
Find the condition number of diag(4,0.5).
Find the minimum-norm solution of x₁+x₂=6.
Why prefer lstsq over explicitly inverting AᵀA?
solutions: Back substitute: theta₂=1; 2theta₁+1=5 gives theta₁=2.
The singular values are 4 and 0.5, so the condition number is 8.
By symmetry or minimizing t²+(6-t)², the solution is (3,3).
A solver handles rank and stability using appropriate decompositions; normal equations can square conditioning, and explicit inversion is unnecessary.
checkpoint: Distinguish problem sensitivity from solver error, and explain what a minimum-norm solution adds to least-squares fitting.

title: Regularization and the cost of overfitting
goal: Understand how a penalty trades fitting error against coefficient magnitude.
exercises: For the scalar example, find theta when lambda=3.
At lambda=1, compute the residual loss and penalty separately.
Why can input rescaling change a ridge fit?
Which split should choose lambda, and which split reports final performance?
solutions: theta=1; residual loss=(1-2)²=1 and penalty=1²=1, totaling 2.
Equivalent prediction coefficients have different magnitudes after rescaling, so the parameter penalty changes.
Use validation to choose lambda. Keep test data for final evaluation after model selection.
checkpoint: Explain why regularization may deliberately worsen training fit while improving predictions, and design a comparison that avoids test-set tuning.

title: Eigenvectors and repeated transformations
goal: Identify invariant directions and predict repeated application of a square map.
exercises: Find eigenvalues and standard eigenvectors of diag(2,-1).
Apply diag(2,-1) three times to (1,2).
Verify that (1,-1) is an eigenvector of [[2,1],[1,2]].
Why is the zero vector excluded from the eigenvector definition?
solutions: Eigenvalue 2 with (1,0); eigenvalue -1 with (0,1).
The product is (1,-1), so its eigenvalue is 1.
It satisfies Av=lambda*v for every lambda and carries no invariant direction.
checkpoint: Predict repeated transformation along independent eigendirections and explain the conditions needed to use an eigenbasis.

title: SVD and low-rank structure
goal: Read a rectangular map as orthogonal directions with nonnegative stretch factors.
exercises: For singular values [6,3,2], find squared rank-1 reconstruction error.
Give reduced-SVD shapes for a 5x3 matrix.
How many numbers store a rank-4 approximation of a 20x30 matrix?
Does smallest reconstruction error guarantee best recognition accuracy?
solutions: Discard 3 and 2: 3²+2²=13.
4*(20+30+1)=204 versus 600 original entries, ignoring metadata.
No. Reconstruction error treats all entries geometrically; task-relevant details may lie in small singular directions.
checkpoint: Draw the three stages of an SVD and calculate the reconstruction error from discarded singular values.

title: PCA, centering and covariance
goal: Derive the direction of maximum centered variance and distinguish PCA from SVD of one image.
exercises: Center the samples (0,2) and (2,4).
Find the sample covariance of those two samples.
For covariance eigenvalues [4,1,0], what fraction of total variance does the first component retain?
Why is PCA not a supervised classifier?
solutions: Mean=(1,3); centered samples are (-1,-1) and (1,1).
N-1=1, so covariance is [[2,2],[2,2]].
Its directions depend on input variation without using class labels; prediction requires an additional rule or model.
checkpoint: Calculate one-dimensional PCA for points on a line, restore the mean during reconstruction, and explain what object each SVD factorizes.

title: Reconstruction error and data leakage
goal: Evaluate compression and build preprocessing that does not learn from held-out observations.
exercises: If discarded singular values are [3,1], find squared Frobenius error.
For N=5,D=2, turn that error into entrywise MSE.
Should validation samples get their own fitted PCA basis?
Name a reason frame-level random splitting can overestimate future performance.
solutions: Divide by 5*2, giving MSE=1.
No. Apply the training-fitted mean and basis; otherwise feature coordinates differ and validation informs preprocessing.
Nearby frames can be almost duplicates. A model may recognize shared scenes rather than generalize to new sequences.
checkpoint: Write a preprocessing protocol and error denominator precisely enough that another learner can reproduce your comparison.

title: Derivatives and local linearity
goal: Derive a derivative from a limit and use it as a local sensitivity.
exercises: Derive the difference quotient for f(x)=x² at a general x.
Find the derivative of 3x²+2x-5 at x=2.
Use a first-order approximation for (4.01)² around x=4.
Differentiate (3x+1)² and evaluate at x=0.
solutions: [(x+h)²-x²]/h=2x+h, approaching 2x as h→0.
The derivative is 6x+2, giving 14.
16+8*0.01=16.08; the exact answer is 16.0801.
The chain rule gives 2(3x+1)*3=6(3x+1), which is 6 at zero.
checkpoint: Explain a derivative using both a limit and a tangent approximation, then state when that approximation can fail.

title: Gradients and directional derivatives
goal: Interpret a gradient as a vector of partial sensitivities and derive a least-squares gradient.
exercises: Find ∇f for f=x²+xy+2y² at (1,2).
For gradient (3,4), find the derivative along unit direction (1,0).
Write the gradient of L=(1/N)||A*theta-b||².
Does a negative directional derivative guarantee a decrease for every step length?
solutions: Partial derivatives are 2x+y and x+4y; the gradient at (1,2) is (4,9).
Dotting with (1,0) gives 3.
∇L=(2/N)Aᵀ(A*theta-b), with the same parameter dimension as theta.
No. It guarantees local decrease for sufficiently small positive steps under differentiability; a large step can overshoot.
checkpoint: Compute an unseen multivariable gradient, then verify the shape and normalization of a regression-loss gradient.

title: Jacobians and computational graphs
goal: Apply the chain rule to vector computations and combine gradients across branching paths.
exercises: Find the Jacobian of f(x,y)=(x+y,x*y).
For z=(2x+1)², compute dz/dx at x=1.
For L=u²+u³, calculate dL/du at u=2.
If y=Ax and ∇_y L has shape (H,1), give ∇_x L and its shape.
solutions: J=[[1,1],[y,x]], with rows indexing outputs.
dz/dx=4(2x+1), giving 12.
dL/du=2u+3u²=4+12=16. Contributions from both branches add.
∇_x L=Aᵀ∇_y L, with shape (D,1) for A=(H,D).
checkpoint: Draw a branching graph, accumulate every path contribution, and use Jacobian dimensions to justify each multiplication.

title: Hessians, Taylor approximations and gradient checks
reading: MML 5.7-5.8; CS205A 12.3.2-12.3.3, with CS205A 1.2 for rounding error.
goal: Use curvature and finite differences to inspect analytic gradients.
exercises: Find the Hessian of x²+xy+2y².
Evaluate the central-difference derivative of w² at w=3 symbolically.
At a stationary point with Hessian eigenvalues (2,-1), classify the curvature.
Give two reasons a correct derivative implementation might fail a numerical check.
solutions: [(3+h)²-(3-h)²]/(2h)=6 for nonzero h in exact arithmetic.
The Hessian is indefinite, indicating a saddle for a smooth nondegenerate stationary point.
A perturbation can cross a ReLU kink, or stochastic evaluations can use different randomness. Extreme h can also produce numerical error.
checkpoint: Perform and interpret a gradient check, then explain why its result depends on smoothness, determinism and step size.

title: Conditional probability and Bayes theorem
goal: Calculate a posterior while keeping base rates and reversed conditionals separate.
exercises: With P(A)=0.3, P(B|A)=0.8 and P(B|not A)=0.2, compute P(B).
Using those values, compute P(A|B).
If A and B are independent with P(A)=0.4 and P(B)=0.5, find their intersection probability.
Why is detector recall different from the probability an alerted image truly contains the object?
solutions: Recall conditions on true objects; the alert probability conditions on predicted positives and also depends on prevalence and false positives.
checkpoint: Solve a new Bayes example with a frequency table, and explain each conditioning direction in plain language.

title: Random variables, densities and expectations
goal: Distinguish a probability mass from a density and calculate an expectation.
exercises: Find E[X] for values 0,2,4 with probabilities 0.2,0.5,0.3.
For uniform X on [0,4], find P(1≤X≤3).
What is P(X=2) for that continuous distribution?
If E[X]=2 and E[Y]=3, calculate E[2X-Y] without assuming independence.
solutions: Density=1/4; interval width=2, so probability=0.5.
Zero; one exact value has zero interval width.
By linearity, 2E[X]-E[Y]=4-3=1.
checkpoint: Explain how a density of 10 can be valid, then compute both a discrete expectation and a continuous interval probability.

title: Variance, covariance and Gaussian noise
goal: Calculate fluctuation and co-variation, and state what Gaussian noise assumes.
exercises: Find mean and population variance of [1,3,5].
If Var(X)=4, find Var(3X+2).
For 16 independent samples each with variance 4, find variance of their mean.
Does covariance zero guarantee independence? Give the lesson’s counterexample.
solutions: Mean=3; variance=(4+0+4)/3=8/3.
Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X), giving 9*4=36.
4/16=0.25, so standard deviation is 0.5.
No. For symmetric X over -1,0,1, Y=X² depends on X even though covariance is zero.
checkpoint: Distinguish population and sample variance, explain a covariance matrix, and list assumptions needed for averaging to reduce uncertainty.

title: Sampling and empirical uncertainty
reading: MML 6.4 and 8.6; revisit CV Appendix B.1.
goal: Measure uncertainty in an evaluation estimate without confusing it with model confidence.
exercises: At p_hat=0.5 and N=100, find the plug-in standard error.
How does standard error change if N is multiplied by four under the same independent model?
Why is the plug-in normal interval unreliable after 3 successes out of 3?
When evaluating many frames from each video, what could be a better bootstrap unit?
solutions: It halves because standard error scales as 1/sqrt(N).
p_hat=1 gives plug-in standard error zero, hiding substantial uncertainty from a tiny sample.
Resample independent videos or groups when within-video frames are correlated and the deployment target is new videos.
checkpoint: Report accuracy with sample size, sampling unit and an uncertainty method, and explain the limits of that evidence.

title: Likelihood and negative log likelihood
goal: Derive common training losses from declared observation models.
exercises: For y=1,p=0.25, calculate binary NLL.
For labels [1,0] and predictions [0.8,0.3], write their summed NLL.
Under fixed Gaussian variance 2, what multiplies the squared residual sum in NLL?
Why cannot the log-variance term be ignored when predicting variance?
solutions: The correct-label probabilities are 0.8 and 0.7, so NLL=-ln(0.8)-ln(0.7)≈0.5798.
It depends on learned parameters. Dropping it would allow increasing variance to reduce the residual term without the proper likelihood cost.
checkpoint: Derive binary cross entropy and Gaussian squared error from likelihoods, and identify the assumptions that make each derivation valid.

title: Priors, MAP and regularization
goal: Connect a parameter preference to a probabilistic prior while tracking loss scales.
exercises: With sigma²=2 and tau²=4, give lambda under the lesson’s summed-error convention.
For a single observation y=6 with both variances equal to 1, find the MAP.
Does MAP supply a full posterior uncertainty distribution?
If a summed data loss is divided by N, how should its penalty coefficient change to preserve the same optimum?
solutions: lambda=sigma²/tau²=2/4=0.5.
Minimize (theta-6)²+theta²; theta=3.
No. MAP supplies a mode; a full posterior or approximation is needed for distributional parameter uncertainty.
Divide the penalty coefficient by N too, so the entire objective is scaled equally.
checkpoint: Derive ridge from Gaussian assumptions and show how mean-versus-sum reduction changes the numeric coefficient.

title: Logistic regression, softmax and cross entropy
goal: Compute stable class probabilities and derive the gradient of a softmax classifier.
exercises: Compute softmax([0,ln 2]).
For those scores and true class 0, find cross entropy.
Write the score gradient for probabilities [0.2,0.7,0.1] with true class 1.
For X=(8,4), W=(4,3), give dW and db shapes.
solutions: Exponentials are [1,2], so probabilities are [1/3,2/3].
Subtract one-hot [0,1,0], giving [0.2,-0.3,0.1]. Its entries sum to zero.
dW=(4,3); db=(3,) when summed over the eight rows.
checkpoint: Implement stable softmax and explain every term and shape in its mean-loss gradient.

title: Splits, bias, variance and calibration
goal: Design an honest evaluation and separate a confident prediction from a calibrated one.
exercises: Which split selects learning rate?
A model is 90% confident on 20 predictions and correct on 12. Give empirical accuracy and confidence gap.
Give an example of leakage before model training.
Can perfect classification accuracy establish perfect probability calibration?
solutions: Validation selects it; training fits parameters and test evaluates the fixed choice.
Accuracy=12/20=0.6; confidence exceeds it by 0.3. The sample is small, so interpret cautiously.
Fitting normalization or PCA on all samples before splitting, or placing near-duplicates across train and test.
No. A model can classify every case correctly while assigning systematically inaccurate probabilities.
checkpoint: Write a complete split protocol and identify a measure of correctness, a measure of probability quality and a source of sampling uncertainty.

title: Gradient descent and optimality
goal: Derive a learning update and its convergence range for a simple quadratic.
exercises: Take one step for (w-3)² from w=1 with alpha=0.2.
For that loss, give the error multiplier at alpha=0.75.
For H eigenvalues [2,10], give the convergence range for the half-scaled quadratic.
Does ∇L=0 prove a global minimum for a nonconvex loss?
solutions: Gradient=2*(1-3)=-4; next w=1.8.
1-2*0.75=-0.5: errors alternate sign and halve in magnitude.
No. It may be a local minimum, maximum, saddle or another stationary point.
checkpoint: Derive rather than memorize a learning-rate range for a quadratic, and separate a stationary condition from a global guarantee.

title: Mini-batch SGD, momentum and adaptive steps
reading: MML 7.1; CV 5.3.6; optional CS231n learning notes.
goal: Explain gradient sampling and track the state of momentum and adaptive updates.
exercises: With N=100 and batch size 20 without dropping samples, how many updates form an epoch?
Under v_next=0.5v+g, start v=0 and apply gradients 4 then -2. Give both velocities.
Why can oversampling a rare class change the optimized objective?
What is Adam’s bias-corrected second moment after its first nonzero scalar gradient g=3?
solutions: 100/20=5 updates.
Uniform averaging over the altered sampling distribution gives the rare class greater weight unless corrected.
v₁=(1-beta2)*9, and correction divides by 1-beta2, giving 9.
checkpoint: Work two momentum updates by hand, explain mini-batch gradient assumptions and state what optimizer history must be preserved.

title: Convexity, curvature and constraints
goal: Recognize convex guarantees and solve a small equality-constrained problem.
exercises: Is f(x,y)=x²+2y² convex? Use its Hessian.
Minimize x²+y² subject to x+y=4.
Minimize (w-3)² subject to 0≤w≤2.
Why need not a constrained minimum have an ordinary zero gradient?
solutions: H=diag(2,4) is positive definite everywhere, so the function is strictly convex.
Symmetry or Lagrange conditions give x=y=2, with value 8.
The nearest feasible point to 3 is w=2, with loss 1.
At a boundary, decreasing directions may be infeasible; constrained optimality only considers allowable movement.
checkpoint: Solve an equality constraint with both geometry and multipliers, and distinguish local curvature from global convexity.

title: Initialization, scaling and training diagnostics
goal: Use controlled experiments to separate a broken computation from poor learning settings.
exercises: What is cross entropy for equal logits over four classes?
Why can identical initialization keep two hidden units redundant?
Under the stated variance approximation, what weight variance preserves linear variance for D=100?
Name two plausible causes of flat training loss.
solutions: ln(4)≈1.3863 for a single correct class.
Their forward activations and backward gradients can be identical, so symmetry persists under updates.
v²≈1/D=0.01 for the simple linear approximation; the ReLU heuristic would differ.
Parameters may not be updating, gradients may vanish, the learning rate may be tiny, or labels may be misaligned. Test rather than infer solely from the curve.
checkpoint: Design a debugging order that verifies computation before changing model complexity, and justify a comparison with controlled conditions.

title: Sampling, aliasing and image coordinates
reading: CV 2.3.1, 3.5.1-3.5.2 and 3.4; revisit the image-coordinate conventions in Lesson 05.
goal: Explain how continuous variation becomes pixels and why lost detail cannot always be recovered.
exercises: Downsample [0,1,0,1,0,1] by taking indices 0,2,4.
Average adjacent pairs in that row before reducing.
Why can cos(2*pi*n) be confused with a constant from integer samples?
Why is averaging class IDs during mask resizing usually wrong?
solutions: The result is [0,0,0].
The result is [0.5,0.5,0.5].
All integer samples equal 1, matching the constant signal exactly.
Class IDs are categories, not quantities to blend; averaging IDs can invent unrelated classes.
checkpoint: Create two different underlying patterns with the same sampled values and explain what an antialiasing filter can and cannot do.

title: Convolution and cross-correlation
reading: CV 3.2 and 5.4; optional CS231n convolutional-network notes.
goal: Calculate local filter responses and distinguish kernel flipping from weight sharing.
exercises: Find valid cross-correlation of [1,3,2] with [1,-1].
Find valid convolution of the same row and kernel.
Find full convolution of [1,2,3] with [1,1].
What is the response of a zero-sum kernel on a constant patch?
solutions: Use flipped [-1,1], giving [2,-1].
The full output is [1,3,5,3].
It is the constant times the coefficient sum, so zero, before bias and boundary effects.
checkpoint: Show the flip convention, compute a response by hand and explain how weight sharing differs from output invariance.

title: Padding, stride, channels and receptive fields
goal: Calculate output and parameter shapes and track receptive-field growth.
exercises: For L=10,K=3,P=0,S=2,d=1, find output length.
Count parameters in a biased 3x3 layer from 4 to 6 channels.
Find receptive-field width after three 3x3 stride-1 layers.
For X=(5,8,8,1), valid 3x3 stride-1 filtering with four kernels, give the output shape.
solutions: Widths are 3,5,7, so the result is 7.
Height and width become 6: (5,6,6,4).
checkpoint: Annotate an unseen CNN with all activation shapes, parameter counts and a receptive-field calculation.

title: Fourier transforms, smoothing and edges
reading: CV 3.2, 3.4 and 3.5; MML 3.7 for function inner products.
goal: Interpret frequency components and connect local filtering with spectral behavior.
exercises: Find the four-point DFT of [2,2,2,2].
What component is nonzero for [1,-1,1,-1]?
For lengths N=5 and K=3, what FFT padding length prevents circular wraparound in full linear convolution?
Why might smoothing harm recognition of tiny objects?
solutions: X_0=8 and X_1=X_2=X_3=0 under the stated DFT convention.
X_2=4; all other components are zero.
At least N+K-1=7.
Small-object structure may depend on high-frequency detail that the smoother suppresses.
checkpoint: Explain DC, magnitude and phase, and state the padding required before using an FFT for linear convolution.

title: Affine layers, activations and expressive power
goal: Write a shaped forward pass and explain why nonlinear activations change what a network can represent.
exercises: For X=(12,8), hidden width 5 and 3 classes, give all weight and activation shapes.
Combine two affine maps y=Ax+b and z=By+c into one.
Apply ReLU to [-2,0,3].
Evaluate the XOR construction at (1,1).
solutions: z=(BA)x+(Bb+c) under column-vector notation.
The output is [0,0,3].
checkpoint: Annotate a forward pass and prove why removing every nonlinearity collapses stacked affine layers into one.

title: Backpropagation through a two-layer network
goal: Derive every weight, bias and input gradient of a small batch network.
exercises: For hidden row [1,3] and G2=[0.2,-0.2], calculate dW2.
If dA1=[2,-3] and Z1=[-1,4], calculate dZ1.
For X=(7,4), dZ1=(7,6), give the first-layer weight-gradient shape.
Why must parameters stay unchanged until their backward sensitivities are computed?
solutions: The outer product is [[0.2,-0.2],[0.6,-0.6]].
The ReLU mask is [0,1], giving [0,-3].
XᵀdZ1 has shape (4,6), matching W1.
All derivatives must refer to the same forward computation; early updates change downstream Jacobians.
checkpoint: Derive the complete backward pass without looking up formulas and justify every transpose, sum and loss-normalization factor.

title: Regularization, normalization and numerical stability
goal: Explain how training aids change a computation and distinguish them from numerical safeguards.
exercises: Differentiate (lambda/2)||W||².
At keep probability 0.25, what happens to a kept activation of 2 under inverted dropout?
For logit z=100 and label y=0, approximate stable binary NLL.
Why should training and evaluation mode be stated for dropout and batch normalization?
solutions: The gradient is lambda*W.
It becomes 2/0.25=8; a dropped activation becomes zero.
NLL≈100 because ln(1+exp(-100)) is tiny.
Dropout randomness and normalization statistics follow different rules in training and evaluation, changing outputs if modes are mixed.
checkpoint: Separate objective changes, stochastic training operations and stable equivalent formulas, and specify their behavior during gradient checking.

title: Autograd compared with your own gradients
reading: MML 5.6; CV 5.3.5; optional PyTorch autograd tutorial.
goal: Use an automatic-differentiation framework as a comparison for a derived computation.
exercises: For L=(wx+b-y)²/2 with x=3,w=2,b=0,y=4, find dL/dw and dL/db.
Why can calling backward twice without resetting gradients change the values you inspect?
What should be compared before comparing gradients?
Why is argmax classification accuracy usually unsuitable as the differentiable training objective?
solutions: z=6 and residual=2, so dL/dw=2*3=6 and dL/db=2.
Many frameworks add newly computed gradients to existing stored ones rather than replacing them.
Forward values, shapes, dtype and the exact loss expression and reduction.
Argmax decisions are piecewise constant and discontinuous at boundaries, giving no useful ordinary gradient for most parameter settings.
checkpoint: Produce a matched hand, numerical and optional framework derivative comparison, and explain why autograd does not guarantee a correct learning problem.

title: CNN classification, inductive bias and augmentation
reading: CV 5.4 and 6.2; optional CS231n convolutional-network notes.
goal: Connect local shared weights to a trainable image classifier, choose label-preserving transformations and reuse a pretrained network.
exercises: Count convolution parameters for a biased 3x3 layer from one to four channels.
For the worked 8x8 CNN, give the flattened feature dimension.
Why does shifting a feature map not imply unchanged class scores?
How should a horizontal flip affect a box [x1,y1,x2,y2] in an image of width W using boundary coordinates?
solutions: The classifier head or pooling/stride/boundary choices may depend on where features occur.
The flipped box is [W-x2,y1,W-x1,y2], with the image and labels transformed together.
checkpoint: Explain an end-to-end CNN forward and backward computation, its parameter count and one task-specific augmentation assumption.

title: Bounding boxes, localization losses and IoU
reading: CV 6.3; revisit CV 5.3.4 for training objectives.
goal: Compute box overlap and distinguish localization training from detection evaluation.
exercises: Convert center (4,3), width 2, height 4 to boundary coordinates.
Evaluate Smooth L1 with delta=1 at residuals 0.5 and 2.
Why should two duplicate boxes not both count as true positives for one object?
solutions: Intersection=1, union=4+4-1=7, so IoU=1/7.
The box is [3,1,5,5].
One ground-truth object can be matched once under the declared protocol; otherwise duplicates would inflate recall and precision.
checkpoint: Calculate a box metric with explicit coordinate conventions and explain the output, training objective and matching rule of a localization task.

title: Segmentation and class imbalance
reading: CV 6.4; revisit CV 5.3.4 for classification losses.
goal: Define pixelwise prediction and explain why background accuracy can mislead.

Does adding rare-class weight leave the original unweighted cross-entropy objective unchanged?

Under channel-last convention, shape is (4,32,48,3).

title: Precision, recall, AP and mask metrics
reading: CV 6.2-6.4; optional official COCO evaluation implementation.
goal: Calculate threshold-based and ranking-based metrics under a declared evaluation protocol.
exercises: For TP=6,FP=3,FN=2, calculate precision and recall.
For ranked outcomes TP,FP,TP and two targets, compute the lesson’s noninterpolated AP.
Why can micro and macro averages disagree on imbalanced classes?
What must be specified before comparing two detection AP numbers?
solutions: Precision=6/9=2/3; recall=6/8=0.75.
Positive ranks have precision 1 and 2/3; AP=(1+2/3)/2=5/6.
Micro pools counts and gives frequent classes more influence; macro gives each included class equal weight.
Class set, matching and duplicate policy, IoU threshold(s), recall interpolation/sampling, size ranges and prediction limits where applicable.
checkpoint: Explain a complete evaluation protocol and compute its small-case metrics by hand, including denominators and matching choices.

title: Controlled comparisons and reproducibility
reading: MML 8.6; revisit the optimization diagnostics from Lesson 32.
goal: Separate a measured improvement from an uncontrolled difference between runs.

Why is changing optimizer and architecture simultaneously hard to interpret?
Does averaging three training seeds remove uncertainty about the test population?
List information needed to reproduce a fitted preprocessing pipeline.
solutions: Mean=0.8; sample variance=(0.01+0+0.01)/2=0.01, so standard deviation=0.1.
The result measures a bundled change, so either factor or their interaction could explain the difference.
No. Training-run variation and test-sampling uncertainty are different and both may matter.
Training split identifiers, scaling/centering statistics, selected feature basis, code and parameter settings.

title: Errors, uncertainty and domain shift
reading: MML 8.6; revisit CV Chapters 5-6 and Lesson 24.
goal: Audit failure patterns and distinguish observed evidence from explanations requiring another experiment.
exercises: Name two different kinds of domain shift for synthetic bars.
Why can unchanged recall coexist with worse precision after a prevalence change?
How would you test whether contrast causes an error pattern?
Does a narrow confidence interval on one test set prove robustness to a new distribution?
solutions: An input shift such as stronger noise, and a prevalence shift such as far fewer vertical bars. Position or label changes are other distinct cases.
Precision conditions on predicted positives and depends on prevalence as well as class-conditional positive and false-positive rates.
Vary contrast while keeping label, position, noise protocol and model fixed; compare errors and counts over repeated generated samples.
No. It addresses sampling uncertainty under its population assumptions, not arbitrary distribution shift.
checkpoint: Deliver three analyzed cases, group-level evidence, one tested explanation and one clearly labeled unresolved hypothesis.

title: Read a method and defend your maths
reading: Revisit the MML and CV sections used by your project; choose one original paper after matching its prerequisites.
goal: Map a research method to a concrete computation and defend the choices in your own project.
exercises: List five items you must identify in a new method.
Distinguish an empirical benchmark result from a mathematical guarantee.
Give a complete input-to-metric explanation of your capstone in five sentences.
Name one next topic and explain which gap in your project motivates it.
solutions: Inputs, parameters, outputs, objective and evaluation protocol, with the assumptions and shapes that define them.
A benchmark result measures a stated procedure on particular data; a guarantee is a conditional logical statement under specified assumptions.
A satisfactory answer declares representation and shapes, forward computation, loss assumptions, training updates and evaluation protocol without skipping preprocessing or selection.
For example, camera geometry is motivated by estimating 3D structure from views; probability calibration is motivated by unreliable confidence. Choose based on a specific need.
checkpoint: Defend your complete project with one worked calculation from each mathematical pillar and a clear account of the limits of its evidence.
